In a quiet neighbourhood outside Manassas, Virginia, there's a sound that never stops. Not a siren. Not traffic. A hum. Day and night. It comes from the building across the road. A building with no windows, no sign, and almost no people. It's a data centre. And it's one of the most boring buildings ever designed. So here's the puzzle. In the first three months of twenty twenty-six, local opposition blocked or delayed about 130 billion dollars of these buildings across the U S. Between April and June, another 68 billion. There are now more than 800 groups fighting them, in every state except Hawaii. Why would anyone get this angry at a box full of computers?

To understand the anger, we have to start with what's inside. Every time you stream a show, send a photo, or ask an A I a question, a computer somewhere does the work. We call that place "the cloud." But the cloud isn't in the sky. It's in buildings like this one. Rows and rows of servers, stacked in racks, running every second of every day. And many of them sit in one place. Look at this. Loudoun County, Virginia. Locals call it Data Center Alley. It has one of the biggest concentrations of data centres on Earth. Why here? It's an accident of history. In the early nineteen nineties, one of the internet's first big exchange points, a place where networks swap traffic, opened just down the road. It was called Mae East. A O L moved its headquarters to Ashburn in nineteen ninety-six. Fibre optic cable followed. And once the cables were there, every new data centre wanted to be close to them. Close to the cables meant faster connections. So they kept clustering. For years, nobody really noticed them. They were quiet neighbours. Then A I changed the maths. Training and running A I models takes enormous amounts of computing, and that takes enormous amounts of electricity. In twenty twenty-three, data centres used about 4.4 percent of all electricity in the United States. By twenty twenty-eight, the government's own researchers think it could be as much as 12 percent. Worldwide, the International Energy Agency expects data centre electricity use to roughly double by twenty thirty. A single new A I campus can now need as much power as a small city. That's the shift. These buildings went from quiet neighbours to some of the biggest customers on the grid. And when something that big plugs into the grid, everyone connected to it feels it. Which brings us to the first reason people are angry. The bill.

Your electricity doesn't just come from a power plant. It comes from a shared system called the grid. And the grid has to be ready for the busiest moment of the year, not the average day. In the eastern U S, a grid operator called P J M keeps that promise for about 65 million people. Once a year, it holds an auction to pay power plants to be available when needed. Think of it like reserving seats for a concert that might sell out. When lots of new people want seats, the price of reserving one goes up. And the new arrivals want a lot of seats. Tech companies are planning data centres that each need hundreds of megawatts. Look at what happened. For 2024 to twenty twenty-five, a megawatt of capacity cost about 29 dollars a day. The next year: about 270 dollars. Almost ten times more. Then: 329 dollars, the maximum allowed. The grid's independent market monitor found data centres were responsible for most of that jump, about 63 percent of the increase in one auction. And who pays for capacity? Everyone on the grid. Including you. Across the region, household supply rates rose by between 5 and 44 percent, depending on the utility. Then there are the wires. New power lines and substations to reach these campuses cost billions, and those costs often get spread across all customers. Utilities and data centre companies argue the big customers pay their fair share, and some states now make them sign special contracts to prove it. But from a kitchen table, it looks simple. My bill went up. The building down the road is new. And nobody asked me. That feeling, of paying for something you didn't choose, shows up again and again. Including in the next thing these buildings need.

Computers get hot. Tens of thousands of chips, packed together, make a lot of heat. One of the cheapest ways to cool them is to evaporate water, like sweat on skin. Most of that water doesn't come back. It turns into vapour and leaves. A typical data centre can use around 300,000 gallons a day. Roughly what a thousand homes use. The biggest can use millions. Now picture that in a place that's already short of water. In twenty twenty-five, a huge project codenamed "Project Blue" came to Tucson, Arizona. Residents packed city meetings. And Tucson's council voted to walk away from it. In Georgia, near a Meta data centre, some neighbours say their wells started failing after construction began. Meta says its own studies found no link. But you can see why people are suspicious. Newer permits there allow for up to six million gallons a day. To be fair, many newer designs use closed-loop cooling that barely consumes any water at all. But that uses more electricity instead. So the problem moves back to the grid. Power or water. Every data centre makes a trade. And the neighbours pay for either side.

Remember that hum? In the Great Oak neighbourhood of Manassas, residents said a nearby Amazon Web Services campus filled their evenings with a constant, high-pitched whir. Fans and chillers on the roof run all the time. The sound doesn't stop at night. Counties in Virginia have been rewriting their noise rules just to keep up. Then there's the air. In South Memphis, Elon Musk's company ex A I built a giant A I supercomputer called Colossus in a matter of months. To power it quickly, it brought in gas turbines, dozens of them. The Southern Environmental Law Center counted 35 running without permits. The nearest neighbourhood, Boxtown, is a historically Black community that already lived with heavy industry. Local officials later granted permits for 15 turbines. Residents and civil rights groups are still fighting. And then there's land. In Prince William County, Virginia, a plan called the Digital Gateway would have covered about 2,100 acres with data centres. Right next to a Civil War battlefield. It would have been one of the largest data centre campuses in the world. Residents sued. A court voided the rezoning, and the developer gave up its appeal. Noise. Air. Land. None of these is new. Factories and highways have caused all of them. The difference is that those things usually came with lots of jobs. Which raises the obvious question. What does a town actually get in return?

Data centres cost a fortune to build. Hundreds of millions of dollars, sometimes billions. But once they're running, they need surprisingly few people. Building one does create jobs: hundreds, sometimes thousands, of construction workers. But those jobs end when the building is finished. Virginia's own auditors found a typical large data centre employs about 50 full-time workers, and around half of them are contractors. Meanwhile, many states hand them big tax breaks to win them. Virginia's sales tax exemption for data centre equipment cost state and local governments about 1.9 billion dollars in twenty twenty-five. One watchdog group worked it out at more than a million dollars for every new job. But here's the other side, and it matters. Virginia's own study found the exemption was one of the state's best-performing incentives, producing about six dollars of labour income for every dollar given up. And look at Loudoun County, Data Center Alley itself. Data centres bring in about 1.3 billion dollars a year in local taxes, around 38 percent of the county's general fund. That money helped cut the homeowner property tax rate every year for a decade. So data centres can be a great deal. For the right place. The catch is that the benefits and the costs often don't land in the same place. The tax money goes to one county. The power lines, the higher capacity prices, the water, spread out to everyone else. And that mismatch is the heart of this story.

Look back at every fight in this video, and there's a pattern. The benefits are global and invisible. Faster apps, smarter A I, profits for some of the biggest companies in the world. The costs are local and very visible. A hum. A bill. A dry well. A field that's gone. And often, residents find out late. Projects arrive with code names, like Project Blue, and details come after the deal is shaped. That's why this fight doesn't split neatly between left and right. Rural conservatives worried about land and taxes are standing next to environmentalists worried about water and gas. And they're winning more often. Around 30 states have now passed rules on where data centres can go and what they can use. Some towns have simply hit pause. Near Detroit, a utility authority voted to stop new water and sewer service to data centres for a year. Meanwhile, the industry keeps planning to build more, and faster, because the demand for computing isn't slowing down. So this isn't really a fight about whether data centres should exist. The phone in your pocket depends on them. So does almost everything online. It's a fight about who pays, and who gets a say.

So is there a version of this that neighbours wouldn't hate? Some places are already trying. Start with the bill. In Ohio, regulators approved a rule for the biggest new data centres. They must pay for at least 85 percent of the power they reserve, for up to 12 years, even if they don't use it. The idea is simple. If you ask the grid to build for you, you pay for it, not your neighbours. Then there's the heat. All that warmth the cooling systems throw away could heat homes instead. In Denmark, Meta's data centre in Odense sends its waste heat into the city's heating network, for up to 11,000 homes. In Finland, Microsoft and the energy company Fortum are building a system to supply about 40 percent of the district heating for around 250,000 people. Other fixes are less glamorous. Closed-loop cooling to save water. Real noise limits. Building next to new power instead of plugging into an already stretched grid. And maybe the biggest one: telling people early. Before the land is bought. Before the deal is done. None of this makes a data centre invisible. But it changes the question from "Why is this being done to us?" to "What do we get, and what does it cost?"

For years, the internet felt weightless. Something that lived nowhere. But it turns out the cloud has an address. It uses power, and water, and land. It makes noise. And more and more, it's somebody's neighbour. The question is whether that neighbour gets to have a say.
